Conformers 20, 16, and 8 are the most convincing low-strain structures: their methyl-to-imine and aldehyde-carbon-to-imine separations are roughly 4.8-5.1 Å, the chain is extended, and neither the methyl group nor the two oxygen atoms is forced into the imidate region. Conformers 26, 10, 29, 7, 25, 17, 11, 2, and 19 retain generally staggered chains and only moderate group approach; their relative order is less certain because some place the ether chain anti to the methyl group whereas others place it anti to the formyl group. Conformers 13, 23, 9, 22, 12, 27, 21, 1, and 14 have increasingly gauche central torsions or shorter methyl/imidate contacts, but still avoid a severe direct clash. Conformer 6 has a notably short O7...O12 contact near 3.2 Å, while 18, 28, and especially 5 bring the imine nitrogen close to the aldehyde carbon or oxygen. No structure shows a strong conventional N-H...O hydrogen bond: the shortest H15...O7 distances are approximately 2.58 Å in 15, 2.73 Å in 24, and 2.98 Å in 3, but the corresponding N-H...O angles are only about 45-70 degrees, far from hydrogen-bond geometry. These apparent contacts are therefore treated as weak and are outweighed by very short N14...C6 approaches: about 2.01 Å in 15, 2.04 Å in 4, 2.07 Å in 24, and 2.13 Å in 3. Conformer 3 additionally has a short methyl-to-N14 distance near 2.86 Å, making it the most crowded. Conformer 30 has a similarly short methyl-to-N14 distance around 2.81 Å despite otherwise separating the polar termini. The bottom group is consequently dominated by 30, 24, 4, 15, and 3. The middle of the ranking is uncertain because intramolecular dispersion can favor somewhat folded geometries, whereas electrostatic separation favors the extended ones; no thermochemical data are available to resolve that balance exactly.

Connectivity (consistent across all blocks): 23 atoms = C8H14O. Atoms 5-10 form a cyclohexene ring (C6=C7 double bond, C5/C8/C9/C10 sp3), C1 is a methyl on C5, and C13-O14-H15 is a hydroxymethyl on C9. There is only ONE oxygen, so a classical intramolecular O-H...O H-bond is impossible; the only possible stabilizing intramolecular contact is a weak O-H...pi (alkene) interaction, which is marginal. Stability is therefore governed mainly by (i) cyclohexene half-chair quality (low ring strain, C=C not twisted), (ii) whether the methyl and CH2OH substituents are pseudo-equatorial rather than pseudo-axial (avoiding 1,3-diaxial/gauche strain), and (iii) absence of short nonbonded H...H / H...C contacts and whether the O-H is folded back into the ring (steric penalty) versus pointing outward. I screened each set for gross compactness (coordinate span as a proxy for folded/clashing geometries), substituent orientation relative to the ring mean plane, and O-H direction. Step by step: (a) Extended frames with both substituents splayed outward and O-H pointing away from the ring (6, 16, 5, 25, 9, 19, 21) show the fewest close contacts and near-ideal half-chairs - placed at the top. (b) 3, 29, 8, 28, 23, 1 are similarly equatorial but with slightly more gauche Me/CH2OH relationships or a mildly twisted alkene, so they follow. (c) 18, 13, 27, 15, 22, 30, 4 are intermediate: one substituent is more axial or the CH2OH C-C-O torsion eclipses a ring bond, giving moderate gauche strain but no severe clash. (d) The lower tier (12, 7, 26, 14, 20, 10, 24, 17, 11, 2) shows one or more penalties: O-H vectors folded back toward the C=C/ring face (26, 14, 20, 10, 24, 11, 12) creating close O...C/H contacts, more compact overall spans (2, 17, 11) implying eclipsed ring bonds and H...H crowding, or a pseudo-axial methyl/CH2OH with 1,3-diaxial-like compression (7, 12). Uncertainty: without energies I cannot resolve the fine spacing within tiers; the biggest error bars are in the middle (roughly ranks 8-22), where several conformers differ only by CH2OH rotation. The bottom few are distinguished more confidently by compact geometries and inward-pointing OH groups.

The molecule is C6H13NO2: an N-formyl amino-alcohol, CH3-CH(CH2OH)-CH2-CH2-NH-CHO, with two H-bonding sites (amide N-H donor / C=O acceptor, and alcohol O-H donor/acceptor). Stability should be dominated by intramolecular H-bonds that close favorable pseudorings: a 6-membered N-H···O(alcohol) ring (N8-H12···O19, path N-C7-C6-C5-C18-O) and an 8-membered O-H···O=C ring (O19-H20···O10=C9). I screened each conformer by the key heavy-atom distances N8···O19 and O19···O10 and by whether the N-H (H12) or O-H (H20) proton actually points at the acceptor (donor-H···acceptor ~1.8-2.1 A, X···Y ~2.8-3.0 A = H-bond; >4 A = no interaction). Clear H-bonded conformers: 6-ring N-H···O in 5,9,14,27 (H···O ~1.90-2.02) and more marginally 16,19,25 (2.03-2.18); 8-ring O-H···O=C in 20,3,7,24,29,28 (H···O ~1.84-1.94) and weaker 4,8,11,17 (1.98-2.11). Conformer 20 has the shortest donor···acceptor contact (~1.84 A) and 5/9/14 have tight 6-ring N-H···O, so these sit at the top; I slightly favor the shortest, best-aligned bonds (20,5,3,7,9) then the other good 8-rings and the remaining 6-ring cases, with 27/16/19/25 lower because their H···O is longer or the angle is poorer. Conformers 6 and 23 have N···O near 2.9-3.2 A but the N-H proton points away from the alcohol O, so they get only partial dipole credit and fall just below the true H-bonded set. The remaining structures (1,2,10,12,13,15,18,21,22,26,30) have the two heteroatom ends 4.3-6.0 A apart (no H-bond); among them I rank less-extended / less-separated ones (23,18,6,26,12) above the most stretched chains, and the most fully extended, heteroatom-isolated geometries (21,10,22,13,2,30) at the bottom. Uncertainties: (i) the N-H···O 6-ring vs O-H···O=C 8-ring trade-off is close, so the exact order inside the top ~17 is soft; (ii) within the non-H-bonded tail the ranking is essentially enthalpic (compact vs extended) and entropic effects are ignored, so that tail (positions ~18-30) is the least reliable part; (iii) borderline cases 4,8,11,16,17,19,25 could plausibly move up or down several places.

Connectivity (same atom order in every block): CH3-C*H(CH2OH)-C*H(OH)-CH-CH2 with an aziridine N bridging the last two carbons (C13-N15 ~1.44 A, C14-N15 ~1.44 A), i.e. a hydroxymethyl + secondary OH on adjacent stereocenters plus a fused aziridine. Since covalent strain (aziridine ring) is identical in all 30, relative stability is governed by (1) intramolecular H-bonds, (2) close nonbonded contacts, (3) gauche/extended arrangement of the bulky groups.

For each conformer I computed O7...O20 (the two OH oxygens), O...N15 distances, donor-H...acceptor distances and angles, and the aziridine lone-pair orientation to judge whether short N...O contacts are bonding or repulsive.

Strong 5-membered-ring O-H...O H-bonds (O...O 2.76-2.83 A, H...O 1.83-2.06 A, O-H...O angle 140-150 deg): conformers 3, 5, 9, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17, 19, 21, 22, 24, 28, 29. Conformer 23 instead has an excellent 6-membered-ring O-H...N H-bond to the aziridine N (O...N 3.04, H...N 2.02 A, near-linear, ~157 deg at H) - the best single interaction found. Weaker/longer H-bonds: 2 (2.87 A), 4 (2.82), 6 (2.82), 11 (2.79 but bent 52 deg), 25 (2.79, bent 49 deg), and 30 (3.02 A, very bent 58 deg - marginal). No H-bond at all: 1, 7, 8, 10, 15, 18, 20, 26, 27.

Secondary contacts: in 3 (2.77), 19 (2.79), 29 (2.78), 28 (2.78), 22 (2.86), 12 (2.89), 21 (2.92), 24 (2.98) the aziridine N sits 2.8-3.0 A from O20, but the N-H never points at O and the N lone pair points AWAY from the O (dot products strongly negative), so these are mildly repulsive lone-pair/lone-pair-type contacts that partly offset the good O-H...O bond. Conformers 17, 16, 14, 5, 9, 13 combine a strong O-H...O bond with a clean N environment (N...O 3.1-3.3 A) - these are the best O-H...O cases. Conformer 23's O-H...N is the strongest individual bond, slightly penalized by an N...O20 2.75 A contact, so I still place it first but not by much. Conformers 2 and 4 have an additional very bent, weak N-H...O contact (H...O ~2.2-2.35 A, ~70 deg) giving small extra stabilization; 6 is clean but its H-bond is only moderate.

Among the H-bond-free conformers (all extended, no clashes worse than C1...C13 ~3.0 A): 26, 27, 10, 1, 18 have the cleanest separations (N...O 3.0-3.2 A, extended anti chains); 20 and 8 are similar; 15 has the methyl somewhat close to the aziridine (C1...C13 3.03 A) plus N...O 3.08; 7 is worst - it has no H-bond AND a repulsive N...O contact at 2.78 A with the N lone pair pointing away from O.

Uncertainty: within the strong-H-bond tier (ranks ~2-13) the energetic differences are probably <1-2 kcal/mol and my ordering relies on subtle H-bond geometry and estimated repulsion penalties; the ordering among the extended no-H-bond conformers (ranks ~22-29) is also soft. The clear robust conclusions: H-bonded conformers (23, 17, 16, 14, 9, 5, 13 at top) > weakly H-bonded (2, 4, 6, 25, 11, 30) > non-H-bonded extended (26, 27, 10, 1, 18, 20, 8, 15) > non-H-bonded with repulsive contact (7 last).

Connectivity (consistent across blocks) is CH3-C(=NH)-O-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-OH, an imidate (methyl 4-hydroxybutyl acetimidate): atoms 1=methyl C, 2=imidate C, 3=imidate N(H atom4), 5=alkoxy O, 6-9=(CH2)4, 10=hydroxyl O (H atom11). Stability is judged only from geometry: (i) E/Z about C2=N3, read from the O5-C2-N3-H4 arrangement — H4 anti to O5 (E) relieves N-H/OR lone-pair and steric opposition and is favored, while H4 syn (Z) puts HN near O5 and is penalized; (ii) an intramolecular H-bond from the folded (CH2)4 terminus, either O10-H11...N3 or N3-H4...O10 (large ~8-membered pseudo-ring) or O10-H11...O5 (smaller ~6/7-membered pseudo-ring), stabilizes a compact conformer if donor-H-acceptor distance is ~1.8-2.4 A and angle is reasonable; (iii) the butylene tether wants anti C-C-C-C torsions, so strongly folded conformers pay gauche/eclipsing and H...H (<~2.2 A) penalties that can erase the H-bond gain; (iv) extended conformers avoid clashes but forfeit the intramolecular H-bond. Reading approximate donor...acceptor and shortest H...H distances block by block: conformers 8, 17, 2, 5, 13 and 9 show the hydroxyl terminus curled back toward the imidate with a plausible O-H...N/N-H...O contact and an anti (E) C=N, so they are placed highest; 16 and 7 are also folded and H-bonded but show slightly tighter CH2/CH2 gauche contacts, so they follow. The middle group (20,14,23,4,26,28,22,29,12,6) are largely E with the chain either extended and clean or only weakly closed (long O...N/O...O ~3 A), giving neither a strong H-bond nor a serious clash. The lower group (15,21,3,18,24,19,10,1,30,27,25,11) combines one or more penalties: Z-like C=N (HN near O5), very extended anti chains that cannot H-bond (27,25,11 are the most stretched, methyl-to-OH end-to-end largest), or compact folds with short H...H/gauche congestion around C7-C8-C9 (10,1,30) without a compensating linear H-bond. Because these are semi-quantitative coordinate reads rather than computed energies, the ordering within each tier is uncertain (several adjacent pairs are essentially degenerate), but the tiering - folded+E+H-bond > extended clean E > Z or clash/fully-extended - is the robust conclusion.

Connectivity is invariant: N≡C–CH2–O–CH2–CH2–cyclopropyl, so the cyclopropane ring strain is essentially constant and ranking is governed mainly by rotatable-bond torsions, gauche/eclipsing penalties, and whether the nitrile/ether ends are forced toward the cyclopropyl group. I used three geometry proxies: (i) C3···C6 distance across C3–O–C5–C6 for the ether-side torsion, (ii) O4···C7 distance across O–C5–C6–C7 for the alkyl/ring torsion, and (iii) N-to-cyclopropyl-centroid separation as a compactness/steric indicator. N···O distance is nearly constant (~3.35–3.43 Å) in all conformers, so dipole/electrostatic differences from the nitrile and ether are secondary; no conformer shows an obvious sub-van-der-Waals heavy-atom clash, but compact folded forms accumulate multiple gauche interactions. Conformers 16, 30, 13, and 6 have both key torsions most nearly anti (C3···C6 and O···C7 about 3.65–3.8 Å) and are therefore the lowest-strain set; 16 and 30 are almost tied and are the most extended. Next are the extended one-gauche forms with anti O–C5–C6–C7 but a gauche ether kink: 23, 5, 28, then less extended anti-O···C7 cases 3, 1, 12, 4, 10. Forms with an anti ether side but gauche O···C7/C–C–C–ring torsion (22, 18, 17, 7, 24, 15) are penalized somewhat more because a C–C gauche interaction and cyclopropyl approach are usually costlier than a C–O gauche kink. The highest-energy group contains multiple gauche/eclipsed relationships and/or folded geometries: 21, 8, 27, 9, 19, 11, 20, 25, 14, 26, 2, and 29. Among these, 29 is the most compact (N-to-ring centroid only ~4.0 Å) with both central torsions gauche, and 2 is similarly folded with a short O-to-ring separation; 26 and 14 are extended end-to-end but still have two unfavorable gauche relationships, so they sit just above the worst pair. Uncertainty is largest within the middle of the ranking and for the near-tie 16/30; small rotations could swap several adjacent positions.

The connectivity is a seven-membered oxepene ring, O11-C12-C4=C5-C6-C8-C10, with a hydroxymethyl substituent C3-O1-H2 attached to alkene carbon C4. Bond lengths are ordinary in all 30 structures, so the ranking is governed mainly by ring torsions, transannular 1,4 distances, the allylic C3-C4 rotamer, and a few oxygen contacts. The C4=C5 bond remains essentially planar and cis in every structure: C12···C6 is about 2.96-3.12 A and the trans substituent pair C3···C6 is about 3.89-3.92 A. Thus alkene twisting is not the main discriminator. The lowest-strain ring family is represented by 22, 23, 20, 18, 19, 30, 17, 10, and 26. Their opposite ring-atom separations are consistently near 3.0-3.2 A and the flexible allylic and saturated torsions are close to staggered, giving a relatively relaxed half-chair. Within that family, 10, 26, and 19 keep the alcohol oxygen comparatively far from the ring ether oxygen, O1···O11 approximately 4.18-4.38 A, and avoid the more folded arrangement. Conformers 20, 18, and 22 have the same favorable ring but fold O1 toward O11 to about 3.62-3.68 A. In 20 the hydroxyl hydrogen is at least weakly directed toward the ether oxygen, although H···O is still long at about 2.9 A and the D-H···A angle is only around 130 degrees; this gives a small compensating attraction rather than a normal hydrogen bond. Conformers 23, 17, and 30 retain the good ring but rotate C3-O1 over the alkene, placing O1 near C5 and its vinylic hydrogen. This is a less favorable allylic rotamer; 23 has the largest O1···C5 separation and is therefore best of these three, while 30 has the shortest hydroxyl-oxygen/vinylic-hydrogen contact. A second ring family, 15, 25, 28, 11, 7, 3, 13, and 29, is more compact: C6···O11 is shortened to about 2.78-2.81 A and C8···C12 to about 2.89-2.92 A, indicating partially eclipsed ring segments, although without a severe heavy-atom clash. I therefore place it below the first family. Within it, 25, 7, 3, 13, and 29 use the better allylic rotamer, with a C-H rather than C-O bond approximately eclipsing the alkene. Conformer 29 is least favorable of this subgroup because O1 is only about 2.55 A from C12 and O1···O11 is only 3.93 A with no compensating hydrogen-bond geometry. Conformers 15, 28, and 11 have the alcohol oxygen over the alkene; 11 is especially compressed, with O1 only about 2.31 A from C5, so it is last in this family. A third family, 24, 8, 12, 21, and 2, combines an elongated C6···O11 span near 3.29 A with short C8···C12 and C5···C10 contacts near 2.80-2.92 A, consistent with a more twisted, higher-eclipsing ring. Among the better side-chain rotamers, 24 keeps O1 farthest from O11. Conformer 12 has a long, bent OH···O contact, H···O about 2.7 A and D-H···A about 130 degrees, which can slightly stabilize its otherwise close O1···O11 arrangement; 8 has similar oxygen proximity without useful hydrogen-bond alignment. Conformers 21 and 2 additionally put C3-O1 over the alkene, with 2 slightly more compressed than 21. The final family, 5, 27, 4, 6, 16, 9, 1, and 14, appears most strained: C6···O11 contracts to about 2.70-2.72 A while C8···C12 expands to about 3.22-3.25 A, corresponding to one near-eclipsed and one strongly twisted ring segment. Within it, 16, 14, 5, 4, 6, and 27 retain the better allylic side-chain rotamer; 27 and 6 are penalized by especially short O1···C12 separations near 2.6 A. Conformers 9 and 1 combine this strained ring with the C-O-over-alkene arrangement, and 1 has the shorter O1···C5 contact, making it the least stable overall. There is no conventional intramolecular hydrogen bond in any structure; apparent OH···O interactions are long and strongly bent. The largest uncertainty is at the family boundaries, particularly 30 versus 25, 11 versus 24, and 2 versus 16, where side-chain sterics could partially offset the ring-strain ordering.

The structures share the same cyclic-ether framework with a hydroxyethyl substituent. Bond lengths are broadly normal, so the ranking is governed mainly by intramolecular hydrogen bonding, side-chain torsions, residual 1,3-diaxial crowding, and close contacts rather than by large changes in bond strain. Conformer 9 is the clear lowest-energy candidate: the terminal alcohol O is only about 2.94 Å from the ring ether O, and the O-H bond points almost directly toward it, giving a strong intramolecular O-H···O bond. Its axial-substituent 1,3 contact is also somewhat relieved, with the relevant side-chain-to-ring-H distance near 3.05 Å rather than the approximately 2.73-2.82 Å found in most structures. Conformer 16 has a similar O···O distance of about 2.95 Å, but the donor-acceptor alignment is less linear and its diaxial contact is tighter, placing it second. In the remaining structures, the two oxygens are at least about 3.8 Å apart, so none has a true hydrogen bond. The most favorable of these have an anti arrangement along the hydroxyethyl C-C bond, indicated by ring-carbon-to-terminal-O distances around 3.74-3.83 Å: conformers 23, 12, 24, 25, 10, 22, 11, 19, and 14. Among them, 23 is especially favorable because the anti chain is combined with a relaxed 1,3-diaxial separation of roughly 3.08 Å. Conformer 11 additionally points its O-H dipole toward the remote ether oxygen, while 22, 19, and 25 combine good anti torsions with relatively unobstructed side-chain placement. Conformer 12 remains competitive despite a tighter side-chain/ring contact; 10, 24, and 14 are progressively less favorable because their rotation about the substituent bond leaves more carbon-carbon gauche crowding. A group of gauche-chain structures follows. Conformers 15, 3, 17, 29, 21, 27, and 7 have favorable or at least nonrepulsive orientation of the O-H dipole toward the ether oxygen, although their O···O separations of roughly 4.7-5.7 Å are too long for hydrogen bonding. Conformer 30 has no useful dipole alignment but has a particularly open side-chain/ring arrangement and an almost ideal gauche torsion. Conformers 28, 2, 6, and 13 are also geometrically reasonable gauche forms but lack the electrostatic advantage. Conformers 4, 1, 5, 8, 18, and 20 place the two oxygen atoms relatively close while pointing the alcohol hydrogen away, creating unfavorable oxygen-oxygen or dipole alignment without hydrogen-bond compensation. Conformer 26 has an intermediate ring-carbon-to-terminal-O distance of about 3.49 Å, consistent with a poorly staggered, strained torsion, together with a close side-chain/ring arrangement and unfavorable oxygen orientation. Conformer 20 is placed last because it combines oxygen-dipole repulsion with a particularly short terminal-O-to-ring-carbon contact of approximately 2.61 Å. The largest uncertainty is in the broad middle of the ranking, especially among conformers 10-24, where anti-chain stabilization, gauche crowding, and weak long-range dipole effects are of comparable magnitude.

The formula is C6H12O2 (6 C, 12 H, 2 O) = one ring; the connectivity traces a cyclohexane-1,3-diol (OH on ring carbons 1 and 3-equivalent). So stability is governed by (i) chair vs twist-boat ring puckering, (ii) axial/equatorial placement of the two OH groups, (iii) possible intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bonding across the 1,3-diol (O1...O11 ~2.8-2.9 A with H pointed at the acceptor), and (iv) nonbonded O...O / H...H clashes when the two OHs are forced near each other without a proper H-bond. I used the O1-O11 separation as the key diagnostic: ~2.8-2.9 A = intramolecular H-bond (stabilizing, cis-1,3 diaxial-like chair); ~6.2-6.6 A = extended diequatorial/trans chair (low strain, no H-bond); ~4-5.7 A = twist-boat/folded or gauche (intermediate); ~3.8-4.3 A where H is not donated = repulsive O...O contact (destabilizing). H-bonded conformers (1, 25, 9, 30; O...O 2.87-2.92 A) rank highest, with 1 and 25 showing the cleanest donor-acceptor geometry. Next are the extended, low-strain diequatorial-like chairs ordered roughly by elongation (15, 23, 10, 18, 26, 20, 3, 4, 22, 21, 8, 29, 6, 16). The mid-distance set (11, 17 ~4.0-4.3 A; 7,5,19,24,2,27,13,14 ~5.1-5.7 A) reflects twist/partially folded rings with gauche OH relationships and more eclipsing. The worst are 12 (O...O ~3.85 A without good H-bond alignment = lone-pair repulsion) and 28 (most compact/folded, ~5.06 A with flagpole-type crowding). Uncertainty is high within the extended-chair block (subtle axial/equatorial differences cannot be resolved exactly from coordinates alone) and in ordering the twist-boat intermediates; the H-bonded top-4 and the strained bottom-2 are the most robust assignments.

Step 1 — Identify the scaffold and possible stabilizing/destabilizing contacts. Each block has 18 atoms: 1 O (atom 1, an aldehyde C=O, atom 2 bearing H atom 18), 1 N (atom 11, secondary amine bearing H atom 12), 7 carbons and 9 H (C7H9NO). The chain reads O=CH–CH2–CH2–C≡C–CH–CH(NH)–…, i.e. an amino‑aldehyde built around a central alkyne (atoms 6–7–8–9). The two obvious handles for relative stability are (a) an intramolecular N–H···O=C hydrogen bond (needs O···N ≈ 2.7–3.2 Å and H(N)···O ≲ 2.5 Å) and (b) steric/torsional strain, which is minimized in extended, anti zig‑zag conformers with a linear alkyne. Because the carbonyl O and the amine N are the two termini, the O···N distance is essentially the end‑to‑end (folding) metric, so I computed it for every conformer from atoms 1 and 11, and H(N)···O from atom 12.

Step 2 — Test for hydrogen bonds. Approximate O···N / H(N)···O distances: Conf 6 = 4.52/3.68 Å (shortest), Conf 30 = 4.68/3.86, Conf 24 = 4.89/4.29, Conf 11 = 5.60, and everything else ≥ ~5.6 Å rising to ~8.3 Å. Critically, even the most folded structures have H(N)···O ≳ 3.7 Å and O···N ≥ 4.5 Å — far too long for an N–H···O hydrogen bond. The rigid, short chain simply cannot close a ring onto the aldehyde. Conclusion: NO conformer gains an intramolecular H‑bond. Therefore folding brings the two electronegative termini (C=O and N–H) together with no compensating H‑bond, giving steric crowding and an unfavorable aligned‑dipole penalty, whereas extension (large O···N) gives anti torsions, a near‑linear alkyne and minimal nonbonded contact. Stability should therefore increase monotonically with end‑to‑end extension, with alkyne linearity as a tie‑breaker.

Step 3 — Apply the metric. Most extended / least strained (O···N ≳ 7.6 Å): 1 (8.29), 23 (8.11), 28 (7.88 — also the cleanest, almost perfectly linear C≡C with atoms 7–9 y,z nearly constant), 5 (7.78), 13 (7.75), 14 (7.72), 4 (7.71), 16 (7.68). I place 28 first because it combines large extension with the straightest alkyne (least bending strain); 1 and 23 follow. Next tier (~6.9–7.4 Å): 25 (7.39), 3 (7.38), 9 (7.37), 7 (7.20), 19 (7.17), 15 (7.06), 21 (6.94), 8 (6.95). Intermediate, mildly buckled (~6.0–6.65 Å): 18 (6.65), 29 (6.65), 27 (6.57), 26 (6.33), 20 (6.21), 12 (6.14), 22 (6.08), 10 (6.08), 2 (6.07), 17 (6.04). Most folded, with C=O and amine ends forced into proximity but no H‑bond payoff (greatest crowding/dipole penalty): 11 (5.60), then 24 (4.89), 30 (4.68) and 6 (4.52) as the least stable.

Uncertainty: the dominant trend (extended anti > folded, since H‑bonding is geometrically impossible) is robust. Ordering WITHIN the four tiers is soft (± a few positions) because I am using end‑to‑end distance as a proxy and did not exhaustively measure every H···H contact or each sp3 torsion; a couple of mid‑tier swaps (e.g. among 18/29/27 or 22/10/2/17) would not change the chemical picture. The placement of the four folded conformers (6, 30, 24, 11) at the bottom is the most confident part after the top tier.

I first inferred the fixed connectivity from repeated short contacts: an oxetane-like ring C4-C6-C14-O17-C4, a hydroxymethyl substituent O1-H2-C3 on C4, and a formylmethyl substituent C6-C7-C8=O9. Thus the largest variable is not the ring strain itself, which is broadly common, but whether the sole OH donor makes a linear intramolecular H bond to the aldehyde carbonyl and whether the three oxygens are forced into close nonbonded contact. Using H2...O9 distance plus O1-H2...O9 linearity, only 30, 23 and 11 have a convincing O-H...O=C bond: 30 is shortest/most linear, 23 is nearly as good, 11 is slightly longer and more bent, so they are the clear top three in that order. Apparent short H2...O17 contacts in many other conformers are mostly bent/perpendicular, so I did not count them as strong H bonds. Among the rest I favored geometries that separate O1 from O9 and keep O1/O9 away from ring O17, since O...O contacts without a linear H bond are repulsive and folded conformers also look more eclipsed around the oxetane substituents. The best non-H-bonded structures are extended/low-dipole ones such as 14, 4, 10, 26, 22 and 24; 16, 6, 2, 28 and 1 are similar but have somewhat shorter O1...O17 or less ideal carbonyl placement. The middle is uncertain because ring pucker and torsional eclipsing are hard to quantify without energies. The lowest group has either short O1...O9 contacts with the OH pointing away, notably 19, 21, 18 and 8, or very short O1...O17/folded contacts, e.g. 13, 25, 12, 27. 8 is worst because O1 and O9 are close while the O-H bond is roughly perpendicular rather than donated, giving repulsion without H-bond compensation.

All 30 share the same strained epoxide-containing skeleton, so the three-membered C-C-O ring penalty is approximately constant and does not by itself order the conformers.
